name: Check Ins, Surveys, and Counselor Triage
title: Check Ins, Surveys, and Counselor Triage
answer: Check ins, surveys, and counselor triage are ways for schools to hear how students are doing and to route the students who need help to a trained adult quickly. They matter because a student who reports feeling unsafe or hopeless needs a same day response from a person, not a trend report weeks later. The tools support this work, but the judgment about who is seen first stays with the counselor.

sections.body: This idea covers three connected practices: short daily or weekly check ins where students say how they are doing, broader climate and belonging surveys, and triage that helps counselors focus on the students with the greatest need. A check in can be as simple as a form asking students to rate their mood or say whether they need to talk with someone. The problem it solves is that schools often learn about struggling students too late, or only through a crisis. Check ins and surveys surface patterns, such as rising stress before exams, while triage makes sure the most urgent requests reach an adult first. Together they give schools an early view of student wellbeing without replacing the human response that serious disclosures require.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom, a teacher can run a quick daily or weekly check in, for example a simple form where students rate their mood or ask to talk with someone. A counselor then reviews trends across a class or grade to spot patterns, such as stress rising before exams. Students who ask to talk should hear from an adult the same day. Climate and belonging surveys work at a broader level, and AI features can group open responses into themes, with a staff member reading a sample in each theme to check that the grouping is fair. For counselors, a request form and scheduling tool lets students book time and shows who needs help first, though the counselor decides the order. The text does not give separate grade band guidance.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea. It describes practice, such as same day contact for students who ask to talk and staff review of themed survey responses, rather than citing research. The closest thing to a finding is the stated risk that a student who reports feeling unsafe or hopeless needs an immediate response from a trained adult, not a trend report weeks later. On that basis, this idea rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Check ins must be handled with care, and students need to know who sees their answers and what happens next. A student who reports feeling unsafe or hopeless needs an immediate response from a trained adult, not a trend report weeks later. Schools should decide in advance who reviews check ins, how often, and what triggers an immediate response. When AI groups open survey responses into themes, a staff member reads a sample in each theme to check that the grouping is fair. Counselors are stretched thin, and while a request form and scheduling tool can show who needs help first, the counselor decides the order using judgment that no form can replace, and a student who writes something alarming in a request should be seen right away.
